title: Megatron Is Moving Fast: What Contractors Need to Know About the Air Force's New Battle Network IDIQ
summary: What Special Notice FA861227RB001 says about the Air Force's Megatron MAC IDIQ, how its timeline compares to Alliant 3, SEWP VI, and ITES-3S, and what to do before the September 30 SOW feedback deadline.
body_markdown:
*What Special Notice FA861227RB001 says, how its timeline compares to other major federal IDIQs, and what to do about it before the September 30 SOW feedback deadline.*


## The short version


The Department of the Air Force has posted a Special Notice for the DAF Battle Network "Megatron"[MAC](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/mac-multiple-award-contract)[IDIQ](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/idiq-indefinite-delivery-indefinite-quantity) (Notice ID FA861227RB001), and the pace of this acquisition is worth paying attention to as much as its scope. The notice itself doesn't state a ceiling, but industry trackers including[DefenseScoop](https://defensescoop.com/2026/09/16/air-force-megatron-idiq-fast-track-daf-battle-network-acquisitions/) and[OST Global Solutions](https://www.ostglobalsolutions.com/air-force-megatron-idiq-new-vehicle-to-replace-abms-and-xa-ordering/) are estimating $4.5B or higher.


**Five things to do this week:**


1. Request access to the controlled draft[SOW](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/sow-statement-of-work) documents through the Attachments section of the SAM.gov notice. Access is vetted against your SAM.gov entity registration and CAGE code, so confirm both are current before submitting the request.
2. Assign someone specific to read the draft SOW in full and complete the government's feedback template, not a general capture note. Feedback and questions are due by **September 30, 2026, at 5:00 PM EDT** , by email to the contracting officer.
3. Map where your technical capabilities, certifications, and past performance do or don't cleanly cover the six scope categories as currently drafted: digital architecture, sensor integration, secure processing, connectivity, applications, and synthetic environment development. Ambiguous or narrow category language is exactly the feedback the government is asking for.
4. Register for the virtual Industry Day ( **October 7, 2026, 8:00 AM–12:00 PM EDT** , Microsoft Teams Live) by the **October 5, 2026, 5:00 PM EDT** registration deadline. One-on-one sessions won't be held, so the live Q&A is the only direct channel to the program office before the draft RFP.
5. Follow Notice FA861227RB001 on SAM.gov directly so amendments reach you automatically. The notice explicitly serves as the acquisition's permanent landing page, and the government expects repeated amendments between now and award.


## What Megatron Is


Per the government's own description, the DBN "Megatron" MAC IDIQ is meant to provide "an agile and competitive contracting framework to rapidly deliver capabilities and address the full spectrum of PAE C3BM requirements throughout the program lifecycle."


It's structured as a hybrid supply-and-service contract vehicle supporting the development, procurement, assembly, delivery, and sustainment of PAE C3BM (command, control, communications, and battle management) product lines.


Under the vehicle, customers will be able to procure capabilities across the six areas above, aimed at integrating Air Force and Space Force C3 programs and delivering what the notice calls "resilient decision advantage."


Megatron will be awarded with two pools: a Small Business pool and an unrestricted pool of awardees. SAM.gov lists it as a Partial Small Business Set-Aside under[FAR](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/far-federal-acquisition-regulation) 19.5, with NAICS code 541715.


The vehicle will be decentralized, meaning any Air Force program office or Department of Defense agency will be able to place[task orders](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/to-task-order) against it once awarded. Source selection will run under FAR Part 15 procedures.


## Why This Notice Is Worth Tracking Closely


The notice explains its own purpose plainly: it's meant to serve as "the official landing page" for the acquisition, and the Notice ID will stay the same throughout every future SAM.gov posting.


The government is explicitly asking industry to "Follow" the notice to get automated updates on schedule changes, draft SOW releases, draft solicitation documents, and Industry Day details. That's a practical signal in itself: the government expects this notice to be amended repeatedly between now and award, so following it is the most reliable way to stay current without checking manually.


## What's Happening Right Now


As of September 4, 2026, the government released the draft Statement of Work for industry review and feedback. The draft SOW and its accompanying feedback template are marked[Controlled Unclassified Information](https://www.goveagle.com/govcon-glossary/cui-controlled-unclassified-information) and require requesting access through SAM.gov, which the contracting team vets against active SAM.gov entity registrations and CAGE codes under foreign participation restrictions.


Feedback and questions on the draft SOW are due by September 30, 2026, at 5:00 PM EDT, submitted by email to the contracting officer.


A virtual Industry Day is scheduled for October 7, 2026, from 8:00 AM to 12:00 PM EDT, held over Microsoft Teams Live. Registration closes October 5, 2026, at 5:00 PM EDT, and the notice specifies that one-on-one sessions won't be scheduled given the expected volume of interest.


The agenda includes an ABMS mission briefing, an informational session on the upcoming RFP led by the Megatron program manager and contracting officer, and a live Q&A, with all questions and government responses compiled and posted back to SAM.gov afterward.


Looking further out, the notice lays out the rest of the schedule: a draft RFP targeted for late Q4 FY26, a final RFP anticipated mid Q1 FY27, and award targeted for Q3 FY27.


## The Pace Is Unusual: Here's the Comparison


Context helps make the point. Large multi-award IDIQs typically take two and a half to three and a half years from first draft solicitation to award.


*The ~12-month Megatron timeline above is the government's current projection, not a done deal. Every vehicle in this chart has slipped its own schedule at least once, so treat this as the plan of record for now and check back closer to Q3 FY27 to see what actually happened.*


Vehicle Draft RFP / solicitation Award Time to award Ceiling


GSA Alliant 3 October 2022 March 2026 ~41 months No stated ceiling (early planning docs floated ~$75B before GSA restructured it as no-ceiling)


Army ITES-3S May 2015 September 2018 ~40 months $12.1B


NASA SEWP VI September 2023 June 2026 ~33 months $60B ($20B across each of 3 categories)


AFLCMC/XA MAC IDIQ March 2022 December 2022 ~8.5 months $900M


Air Force ABMS February 2020 (BAA) May 2020 ~91 days $950M


DAF Battle Network "Megatron" August 2026 (Special Notice) Q3 FY27 (targeted) ~12 months (projected) Not stated in the notice; industry estimates put it at $4.5B+


GSA's Alliant 3, one of the largest IT vehicles in government, took roughly 41 months from its October 2022 draft RFP to its March 2026 award. NASA's SEWP VI took about 33 months from its September 2023 draft RFP to its June 2026 award. The Army's ITES-3S vehicle took even longer, about 40 months from its 2015 draft RFP to award in 2018.


In each case, the gap was driven largely by extended question-and-answer cycles, repeated deadline extensions, and lengthy evaluation periods once proposals were finally submitted.


Ceiling size doesn't track cleanly with pace. Megatron's projected $4.5B+ estimate sits well below Alliant 3 and SEWP VI, which took years, but also well above the $900M-$950M ceilings on XA MAC and ABMS, the two vehicles that moved in months rather than years.


Megatron is trying to hit an XA MAC/ABMS-speed timeline at something closer to ITES-3S scale, using the slower of the two evaluation paths. That combination, not the dollar figure on its own, is what makes the schedule worth watching.


Megatron's own predecessor vehicles inside the Air Force moved much faster, though it's worth being precise about why.[Red Team Consulting's reporting](https://redteamconsulting.com/2026/09/14/air-force-megatron-idiq/) notes that Megatron is explicitly meant to supplement, and eventually take over ordering from, two existing Air Force vehicles: the ABMS IDIQ and the XA IDIQ. That matters for the pace comparison, because Megatron isn't defining a mission area from scratch; it inherits scope and vendor-pool knowledge those two vehicles already built.


- **AFLCMC/XA MAC IDIQ:** March 2022 solicitation to first awards in December 2022, about eight and a half months, using a simplified evaluation structure to onboard 93 companies quickly.
- **Air Force ABMS:** February 2020 Broad Agency Announcement to first awards in May 2020, roughly 91 days, running as an open BAA with continuous on-ramps rather than a traditional FAR Part 15 competition.


That last detail is the one worth sitting with. Both of Megatron's fast predecessors hit their numbers by using a lighter-weight process: a BAA for ABMS, a simplified structure for XA MAC, rather than a full, traditional competition. Megatron, by contrast, is running under Part 15 source selection procedures, the more rigorous and traditional evaluation path.


Targeting roughly a year from its August 2026 Special Notice to a Q3 FY27 award while using the heavier process is a more demanding pace than what its predecessors achieved, even accounting for the head start that comes from consolidating two already-mature vehicles rather than building a new mission area from zero. It's also still dramatically faster than Alliant 3, SEWP VI, or ITES-3S.


For companies used to the slower pace of those vehicles, the adjustment to make is the same either way: this is moving on an Air Force clock, not a GSA or Army one, and the compressed timeline is deliberate rather than incidental.


## What Changes for Your Capture Team


**The window is short and the deadlines are real.** Unlike a vehicle still years from a draft RFP, Megatron gives you two concrete near-term chances to shape scope before it locks: SOW feedback due September 30, and the Industry Day Q&A on October 7. Both close within the next three weeks. Treat them as capture, not just compliance.


**The scope categories are still movable.** Because the six categories (digital architecture, sensor integration, secure processing, connectivity, applications, synthetic environment development) are out for comment, this is the point where a category definition that excludes work you actually do can still be fixed. After the draft RFP in late Q4 FY26, that window closes.


Running your organization's certifications and past performance against each of the six categories is the same exercise as a compliance matrix, just done a step earlier than usual, against a draft SOW instead of a live Section L/M. GovEagle's SOW and requirements extraction can generate that first-pass mapping directly from the draft document, so the feedback you submit by September 30 comes from an actual gap analysis rather than a skim.


Pro Tip


If a category definition looks ambiguous or seems to exclude relevant work you do, that's exactly the kind of feedback the government is asking for in the SOW comment period. Vague feedback ("this scope is too narrow") gets far less weight than specific feedback tied to a category name and a capability you can point to.


**Past performance sourcing starts now, not at RFP.** Whichever categories your team ultimately pursues, the strongest support will be prior ABMS or XA work, existing C3BM relationships, or Battle Network integration experience. Searching your own past proposals, case studies, and performance records for the right examples is exactly the kind of task GovEagle's content library search is built to speed up, rather than relying on memory or a manual search through SharePoint.


**Re-run the mapping every time the notice is amended.** The government has said outright it expects to amend this notice repeatedly, and the scope categories are still being shaped through the feedback process. A capability mapping done once in September may not hold by the time the draft RFP appears in Q4 FY26.


Re-running that mapping by hand each time it changes gets tedious enough that it often gets skipped.
